title: Make Yourself Visible
intro: When you need to be found, visibility matters more than movement. A clear, deliberate signal is easier to notice than random activity.
steps: Choose an open area whenever it is safe to do so, especially if rescuers may approach from the air.
Use bright or strongly contrasting material that stands out from the surrounding terrain.
At night, use controlled flashlight flashes rather than leaving the light pointed in one direction.
Keep signaling equipment close so you can react quickly when you hear or see rescuers.

title: Stop Before You Get More Lost
intro: Uncertainty becomes harder to fix the farther you continue moving without a confirmed direction.
steps: Stop as soon as the surroundings no longer match what you expected.
Identify the last location you recognized with confidence.
Compare your map, compass and visible terrain before choosing the next direction.

title: Use Landmarks, Not the Needle
intro: A compass gives you direction, but constantly staring at it makes walking less efficient and can distract you from the terrain.
steps: Set your bearing and select a recognizable object directly ahead.
Walk toward that object while keeping your attention on the ground and surroundings.
Recheck the compass when you reach the landmark, then choose the next one.
Use more frequent checks when visibility becomes poor.

title: Save Your Phone Battery
intro: A phone can be useful for maps, communication, light and emergency information, but only while the battery lasts.
steps: Lower screen brightness when maximum brightness is unnecessary.
Use airplane mode when you do not need an active network connection.
Avoid repeatedly opening high-power apps just to check your location.
Keep the phone protected from extreme cold, which can temporarily reduce battery performance.
Reserve enough power for communication or navigation if conditions become more serious.

title: Whistle Before You Shout
intro: A whistle can produce a sharp, repeatable signal without exhausting your voice.
steps: Keep the whistle somewhere immediately accessible rather than buried inside a backpack.
Use deliberate repeated patterns with clear pauses.
After signaling, stop and listen for a response before repeating.

title: Read a Trail in Both Directions
intro: A route can look completely different when you turn around. Remembering the return view makes retracing your path much easier.
steps: Occasionally look behind you while travelling.
Notice distinctive junctions, rocks, bridges, clearings and changes in vegetation.
Pay special attention immediately after major turns.
Take a quick reference photo when a confusing junction may be difficult to recognize later.

title: Keep the Compass Clear
intro: Magnetic interference can make an otherwise correct compass reading misleading.
steps: Move the compass away from phones, speakers, magnets, vehicles and large metal objects.
Hold it level and allow the needle to settle before reading the bearing.
If the reading seems unusual, move several steps away from nearby equipment and check again.

title: Make Morse Rhythm Consistent
intro: Correct symbols are only part of Morse communication. Consistent timing makes the message much easier to recognize.
steps: Keep every dot approximately the same short length.
Make each dash approximately three times the duration of a dot.
Use clear pauses so the receiver can distinguish individual letters.
Slow down before sacrificing rhythm for speed.

title: Use Large Features First
intro: When trying to determine your position, large terrain features are usually easier to identify reliably than small details.
steps: Look first for rivers, ridges, coastlines, major roads or large clearings.
Match several visible features with the map rather than relying on only one.
Use smaller landmarks only after the general area has been confirmed.

title: Signal From the Best Position
intro: A strong signal from a hidden location can be less effective than a simple signal from somewhere clearly visible.
steps: Avoid signaling from behind dense vegetation or terrain when a safe open position is nearby.
Consider where rescuers are most likely to approach from.
Keep visual signals separated from clutter so their shape and movement are obvious.
If you hear an aircraft or vehicle, prepare the signal before it reaches your position.

title: Check the Return Bearing
intro: Knowing the opposite direction of travel can be useful before you commit to a route.
steps: Add 180° to a bearing below 180°.
Subtract 180° from a bearing above 180°.
Record the return bearing when travelling toward a feature that may be difficult to relocate later.

title: Keep Signal Flags Easy to Read
intro: Signal flags communicate best when their colors, order and separation remain clearly visible.
steps: Ensure the flags are not wrapped around the halyard or hidden behind each other.
Read multi-flag hoists from top to bottom.
Do not assume that the meaning of a multi-flag code is simply the meanings of the individual flags combined.
Learn the most important individual flags before moving on to larger code groups.

title: Use a Catching Feature
intro: A catching feature is an obvious landmark beyond your destination that tells you when you have travelled too far.
steps: Choose something difficult to miss, such as a road, river, coastline or major ridge.
Identify it on the map before beginning the navigation leg.
If you reach it unexpectedly, stop and reassess rather than continuing farther.

title: Keep Your Light Useful
intro: A flashlight is most useful when it provides enough illumination without destroying your awareness of the surroundings.
steps: Use only as much brightness as the situation requires.
Avoid shining directly into another person’s eyes.
Give your eyes time to readjust after using a bright beam.
Carry a backup light when travelling in conditions where darkness is expected.
Check battery condition before leaving rather than discovering a problem after dark.

title: Do Not Trust a Single Clue
intro: One observation can be misleading. Direction becomes much more reliable when several independent clues agree.
steps: Compare the compass with terrain and map information.
Treat the Sun, stars and natural features as supporting clues rather than perfect replacements for navigation tools.
If two sources strongly disagree, stop and determine why before continuing.

title: Mark Important Changes
intro: A few useful reference points are easier to remember than every meter of a route.
steps: Note when you cross a stream, road, ridge or other major feature.
Remember major changes of direction.
Record unusual landmarks that would also be recognizable on the return trip.
Use these points to mentally divide a long journey into shorter sections.

title: Confirm Before You Turn
intro: A wrong turn at a junction is much easier to prevent than to correct several kilometers later.
steps: Stop briefly at major intersections and compare the available paths with your map.
Check the expected direction with your compass before choosing a branch.
Look for terrain features that should appear shortly after the turn.
Remember what the junction looks like from the opposite direction in case you need to return.

title: Keep Morse Messages Short
intro: Short, clear messages are easier to transmit accurately by sound, light or vibration.
steps: Remove unnecessary words before transmitting.
Separate letters and words with consistent pauses.
Repeat important information when accuracy matters.

title: Find a Better Observation Point
intro: Sometimes the easiest way to solve a navigation problem is to improve what you can see.
steps: Move only to a nearby safe location with a clearer view.
Look for large features such as ridges, towers, roads, coastlines or valleys.
Compare at least two visible features with the map before deciding your position.

title: Protect Your Map
intro: A damaged map can become difficult to use exactly when you need it most.
steps: Keep paper maps inside a waterproof cover or sealed transparent pouch.
Fold the map so the current area remains accessible without opening the entire sheet.
Avoid placing wet equipment directly on printed map surfaces.
Carry critical coordinates or route information separately as a backup.

title: Check Your Bearing Twice
intro: A few seconds spent confirming a bearing can prevent a long correction later.
steps: Read the degree value once after setting the compass.
Recheck the needle alignment before starting to move.
Confirm that the direction-of-travel arrow points toward the intended side of the route rather than its opposite.

title: Use Sound Carefully
intro: Sound can attract attention when visual contact is impossible, especially in darkness, vegetation or uneven terrain.
steps: Produce clear, intentional signals rather than continuous random noise.
Pause between signal sequences so you can hear a response.
Remember that wind, terrain and buildings can change how sound travels.
Move to a more open position when safe if surrounding obstacles heavily block the sound.

title: Learn the Most Important Flags First
intro: You do not need to memorize the entire International Code of Signals at once.
steps: Begin with high-value individual meanings such as Oscar, Victor, Whiskey, Alfa and Uniform.
Associate each flag pattern with both its phonetic name and meaning.
Practice recognition without showing the letter name.
Add numeral pennants only after the core alphabet flags feel familiar.
Review similar-looking designs together so they become easier to distinguish.

title: Use the Map Scale
intro: A map can tell you much more than direction when you understand its scale.
steps: Identify the map scale before estimating any distance.
Measure the route rather than only the straight line when the path curves significantly.
Remember that steep terrain can make travel time much longer even when map distance is short.

title: Choose an Attack Point
intro: A small destination becomes much easier to find when you approach it from something large and unmistakable.
steps: Select a nearby road junction, bridge, hilltop or other obvious feature.
Navigate confidently to that feature first.
From there, use a shorter and more precise bearing toward the final destination.

title: Keep Your Signal Light Ready
intro: A flashlight can become a communication tool as well as a source of illumination.
steps: Learn how to access its controls quickly before you need them.
Use clear short and long flashes when intentionally transmitting Morse.
Avoid unnecessary continuous use if preserving battery power is important.
Keep the lens unobstructed and clean enough to produce a visible beam.

title: Notice Changes in Terrain
intro: Changes in the landscape can confirm where you are even when individual landmarks are difficult to recognize.
steps: Notice transitions from forest to open ground.
Pay attention when a climb becomes a descent.
Record major stream, road or ridge crossings mentally or in your notes.
Compare these transitions with the expected sequence shown on your map.

title: Do Not Rush a Compass Reading
intro: A compass works best when you give the magnetic needle enough time to settle.
steps: Hold the compass level.
Stop moving while taking an important reading.
Keep it away from obvious magnetic interference.
Repeat the measurement if the needle behaves unusually.
Compare repeated readings before trusting a major change in direction.

title: Build a Simple Route Plan
intro: A route is easier to follow when it is divided into recognizable sections instead of treated as one long journey.
steps: Break the route into legs between major landmarks.
Assign a direction or bearing to important legs.
Estimate the approximate distance of each section.
Identify a feature that should confirm the end of each leg.

title: Share Location Information Clearly
intro: Coordinates are useful only when the receiver understands exactly what format you are using.
steps: State the coordinate format when ambiguity is possible.
Read numbers slowly and verify important digits.
Include a nearby recognizable landmark when available.
Repeat critical location information once to reduce transcription errors.

title: Use Contrast for Ground Signals
intro: A large ground marker is useful only if it can be distinguished from the surrounding terrain.
steps: Use light material on dark ground or dark material on pale ground.
Prefer simple shapes that remain recognizable from a distance.
Keep the area around the signal reasonably clear so its outline is visible.
Make the marker as large as available materials and safe conditions reasonably allow.

title: Practice Without Looking at the Answer
intro: Recognition becomes faster when you actively recall a signal instead of repeatedly rereading it.
steps: Look at a Morse pattern and say the character before revealing the answer.
View a signal flag and recall its name and individual meaning.
Convert simple bearings into compass directions mentally.
Repeat difficult items more often than those you already know well.
Mix Morse, flags and navigation questions so recognition works outside a fixed sequence.
